contributions.statement: In a developer-defined workflow graph with LLM nodes (for example an ingestion pipeline that classifies or summarises content), log each node's inputs, outputs, status and config as a structured record and attach per-node contract assertions (required fields present, ordering after its upstream, consistency with upstream inputs); localize failures by checking those assertions, not by reading the raw run log.
contributions.evidence: §III-B, Table III: same GPT-5.2 pipeline with vs without the symbolic per-node trace and assertions; failure attribution 84.4% vs 59.8%, root cause 87.9% vs 58.3%, repair success 71.3% vs 47.0% on 443 human-labelled Dify/Coze/n8n failures. Three runs averaged, no spread, single model.

contributions.statement: Before re-running an LLM-patched workflow, validate the patched graph structurally (every node reachable, rewired dependencies consistent, configs schema-valid) and reject failing candidates without execution.
contributions.evidence: §VII-A: the four-part pre-execution check agrees with dynamic re-execution at 99.7% precision and 84.6% recall (no counts); the §VI case shows a wiring error caught pre-execution; §VII-C reports 17K tokens per repair.
relative_to: schema/DAG validation before deploy in workflow engines (Airflow DAG import checks, n8n/Dify config validation)

reason: Only the per-node trace plus contract result is isolated, and after the audit it is weak (single model, no spread, own dataset), so it stays a hypothesis. It is the useful half of a static-graph design: node contracts the team could derive from specs. Automated LLM repair of the graph is not shown safe, since the success oracle is undefined and the lead depends on test-set-accumulated experience.
